== Biography ==
'''James Glasgow''' was recorded in the Glencorse baptism register on 14 February 1720, a son of Robert Glasgow and Margaret Davidsone.<ref name="James1720">Scotland's People, Church of Scotland old parish registers, James Glasgow, 14 February 1720, parents Robert Glasgow and Margaret Davidsone, Glencorse parish 687, reference 10/121.</ref>

== Research Notes ==
=== Individual father review, 22 October 2026 ===

The existing father [[Glasgow-3011]] is assessed at 86% (probable). James’s 1720 Glencorse baptism names Robert Glasgow and Margaret Davidsone; the 1704 local Robert/Margaret Davidson marriage identifies a specific preceding couple. The existing 1676 Robert child is a feasible27-year-old groom and the preferred local profile.

Complete profile placement86%; the marriage-to-baptism couple is strong, while Robert’s own child-to-adult identity is inferred. Original uninspected.

Next useful test: Compare the 1676 and 1704 originals for family or residence identifiers.

Source basis already held: [https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-2868 WikiTree profile export for Glasgow-2868]. No new original inspected; no new father attached.


=== Selected uncertain family — 16 October 2026 ===

[[Glasgow-2868|James Glasgow, Glencorse and Cecil accounts]] is selected as the very uncertain working father of [[Glasgow-395|Robert Glasgow, husband of Apphia Moores]]. The preferred model identifies [[Moores-284|Apphia Moores]]’s husband with the Robert Glasgow who acted jointly with Joshua Hartshorn over a Cecil County plantation in 1786, then places him in the local [[Glasgow-2868|James Glasgow, Glencorse and Cecil accounts]]–[[Hartshorne-320|Ann Hartshorne]] family. The joint Glasgow/Hartshorn association gives a more specific family-network clue than surname and county alone. Robert’s estimated circa 1750 birth also fits James’s circa 1720 generation and the existing Cecil children’s mid-century dates. The Harford family context and Cecil land occurrence concern neighboring Maryland counties. This is a conditional reconstruction, not a father statement in either notice.

Two uncertainties are combined: whether the 1786 Robert is Apphia’s husband, and whether that man was a son rather than another relative or associate of James and Ann. Robert’s birth circa 1750 and death circa 1800 are profile estimates, not independently recorded events. The Maryland State Archives biography summarises a Cecil probate family with parents James and Ann, but does not name Robert among their children. That omission is counterevidence; the summary is not established as a complete list of every child. A nephew, cousin, another older Glasgow household or a business relationship remains possible. The 1786 notice does not identify an estate, owner, executor or relationship to Joshua. Its date after the reported 1784 deaths makes an estate explanation possible, without proving it.

The Scottish and Maryland James identities remain uncertain. The Glencorse baptism of 14 February 1720 names Robert Glasgow and Margaret Davidsone, but no cited contemporary record carries that child to the Cecil family. The new parent hypothesis uses the existing colonial family account represented by [[Glasgow-2868|James Glasgow, Glencorse and Cecil accounts]]; it does not prove the migration or strengthen his parents. The 1786 Robert could instead be [[Glasgow-2425|Robert Glasgow, older American account]], whose older estimated generation and broad American context remain compatible with the notice but lack a Maryland household link. That adult-identity alternative is retained without fitting the older man into the new circa 1750 son generation. No existing ancestor, spouse or child attachment is removed or upgraded.

Two very uncertain parent hypotheses join one existing seven-profile family to the working tree. They are one shared family reconstruction, not two independent proofs. No new person, merge, original manuscript inspection, live WikiTree save or certainty upgrade is claimed. The confidently marked measurements remain unchanged, and working connectivity does not validate the inherited Scottish–Maryland identity. Ann’s unsupported local birth estimate is corrected to unknown; the captured WikiTree fields remain unchanged. [https://glasgow.phenotype.dev/people/glasgow-395.html Full selected model, competing families and source limits]. <ref>Previously inspected notices and captured/archival family accounts: [https://www.newspapers.com/image/41024006/ Pennsylvania Gazette,15 February 1786,p.1: Cecil plantation notice, previously inspected original; no kinship stated]; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/41024088/ Pennsylvania Gazette,1 March 1786,p.4: second issue of the same plantation notice, previously inspected]; [https://msa.maryland.gov/megafile/msa/speccol/sc3500/sc3520/017100/017195/html/17195bio.html Maryland State Archives,Samuel Glasgow,MSA SC 3520-17195,Owen Lourie 2016: authored probate summary,read 16 October 2026; original wills not inspected]; [https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/105585399 Baltimore Gazette & Daily Advertiser,23 June 1837,p.4,col.5,as cited in the captured Robert/Apphia biographies; image reference Find a Grave 105585399,not newly inspected]; [https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Glasgow-2868 James Glasgow profile: preserved Glencorse OPR 687,10/121,14 February 1720 citation and unresolved colonial identity]. No original manuscript newly inspected; notice, maternal-surname and Scottish–Maryland identity limits remain explicit.</ref>


The baptism proves the Scottish child and identifies his parents by name. It does not identify his father as [[Glasgow-2867|Robert Glasgow]], master of the ''John and Archibald'' in 1754; that shipmaster identification is unsupported and should remain uncertain.

[[Glasgow-3011|Robert Glasgow (1676-)]] is the probable candidate for the Glencorse father: he is the only indexed Robert Glasgow baptism in Glencorse from 1640 to 1690.<ref name="Robert1676">Scotland's People, Church of Scotland old parish registers, Robert Glasgow, 29 December 1676, parents John Glasgow and Margaret Currie, Glencorse parish 687, reference 10/8; exact-name search for local Robert Glasgow baptisms, 1640–1690.</ref> A same-name man married [[Davidson-20783|Margaret Davidson]] there on 8 June 1704.<ref name="GlencorseMarriage1704">Scotland's People, Church of Scotland old parish registers, Robert Glasgow and Margarett Davidson, 8 June 1704, Glencorse parish 687, reference 20/53.</ref> The marriage index supplies no age, parents, or occupation, so this is not proof of identity. Any future controlled replacement of Glasgow-2867 with Glasgow-3011 must retain an uncertain father relationship.

No cited contemporary record carries the 1720 Glencorse child to Cecil County, Maryland, identifies Ann Hartshorne as his wife, or identifies the attached colonial children as his. The existing colonial dates, location, and relationships should remain uncertain until a migration, marriage, land, probate, or other continuity record identifies this Scottish man.

=== Possible James Glascow, Fogs Manor postal addressee ===
James Glascow, Fogs Manor, is listed among letters remaining in the Philadelphia post office.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/39395391/ The Pennsylvania Gazette, 1757-04-07, p.1].</ref>

Fogs Manor is the printed address qualifier. A neighbouring "Phil. Co." in a separate alphabetic column is not this man’s address. The list states no occupation, so it does not identify him as the later Greenwich Packet master.

This may concern [[Glasgow-2868]]. Exact birth 14 Feb 1720; death c.1784 estimated in Cecil County, Maryland. A 1777 master record precedes estimated death and is not a hard contradiction, but this recorded Maryland trajectory and approximate death deserve review before any association. The postal record states no occupation.

=== Possible James Glascow, master of Greenwich Packet ===
Greenwich Packet: James Glascow, master; James Young, owner; from Philadelphia to Winyew, Carolina; with rum, bread, flour and porter.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/34421452/ The Public Advertiser, 1777-05-14, p.2].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/396765804/ The Ipswich Journal, 1777-05-17, p.1].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/971522063/ The Gloucester Journal, 1777-05-19, p.1].</ref>

James Young is the separate vessel owner, not another form of the master’s name. Three issues repeat one voyage report. Neither the route nor the cargo establishes the master’s family or identifies him with the 1757 Fogs Manor addressee.

This may concern [[Glasgow-2868]]. Exact birth 14 Feb 1720; death c.1784 estimated in Cecil County, Maryland. A 1777 master record precedes estimated death and is not a hard contradiction, but this recorded Maryland trajectory and approximate death deserve review before any association.

=== Possible James Glasgow, Hackman affair witness, 1779 ===
James Glasgow and Andrew Doyle, styled chairmen, are named among persons examined in the Hackman/Miss Ray affair; Glasgow reportedly removed the pistol and gave it to Halliburton.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/970974651/ Gloucester Journal, 1779-04-12, p.3].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1211966255/ Berrow's Worcester Journal, 1779-04-15, p.1].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/396539533/ Jackson’s Oxford Journal, 1779-04-10, p.3].</ref>

"Chairmen" is the recorded word, not a statement that James chaired a meeting. The account gives no age, parents or connection to the American and maritime namesakes.

This may concern [[Glasgow-2868]]. Adult chronology permits 1779; no London witness connection, and later Maryland context remains a competing lead.

=== Possible James Glasgow, Lancaster postal addressee, 1773 ===
James Glasgow (2) is listed among letters remaining in Lancaster’s post office.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/39403087/ The Pennsylvania Gazette, 1773-07-21, p.4].</ref>

The office heading does not establish James’s household or county of residence, and the printed "(2)" does not distinguish a second man of that name.

This may concern [[Glasgow-2868]]. Compatible adult lifespan and later Cecil County context; no Lancaster letter-list connection.

=== Possible James Glasgow, Marsh creek Carlisle list, 1795 ===
James Glasgow, Marsh creek, appears in a Carlisle names/address list reprinted in July–August 1795.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1033874474/ Kline's Carlisle Weekly Gazette, 1795-07-15, p.3].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1033874483/ Kline's Carlisle Weekly Gazette, 1795-07-29, p.4].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1033874491/ Kline's Carlisle Weekly Gazette, 1795-08-12, p.4].</ref>

The three issues repeat one list. The Marsh creek qualifier is not evidence of kinship or continuity with the Lancaster and North Carolina namesakes. Postal correspondence can remain after an addressee’s death.

This may concern [[Glasgow-2868]]. Exact 1720 birth and estimated c.1784 death; weak chronology and regional comparison only, not an exact death exclusion or Marsh creek match.

James Glasgow, living at Christiana Bridge, signs a notice dated 12 March 1785 offering a complete tanyard in the borough of Wilmington, State of Delaware, then in the tenure of Thomas Glenn.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1034008744/ The Pennsylvania Journal, or, Weekly Advertiser, 1785-03-23, p.2].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1034008777/ The Pennsylvania Journal, or, Weekly Advertiser, 1785-03-30, p.1].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1034008853/ The Pennsylvania Journal, or, Weekly Advertiser, 1785-04-09, p.4].</ref>

The 1785 notice explicitly says State of Delaware. Neither notice proves that the advertiser owned the land or worked as a tanner, that the sale completed, or that both notices concerned precisely the same plot. Thomas Glenn is named only in the later notice, while Charles Whitlock belongs to the earlier property description.

This may concern [[Glasgow-2868]]. Adult chronology and later Cecil Maryland regional context are compatible with nearby New Castle, without a Wilmington/Christiana Bridge or property connection.
